1.title: Smallpox and the Development of Vaccination

paragraphs.text: Nobody wants to get sick. Diseases can be scary, and some have no cure. Today we can prevent many diseases, but in earlier times people were not so lucky. Smallpox, for example, plagued people for thousands of years. Learning how to prevent this disease led to the development of vaccination, which now prevents many more diseases.

Smallpox was a highly contagious illness. It usually started with fever and vomiting, and soon a rash would appear. The rash eventually formed scabs that left horrible scars when they fell off. Smallpox also blinded people and killed 30 percent of its victims.

Smallpox was just one of many illnesses caused by viruses. Viruses are extremely tiny organisms that take over living cells. To reproduce, they force those cells to make more of the virus. Ancient people didn't know about viruses. But they did notice that people who survived smallpox usually didn't get it again. They were immune to smallpox even if they were re-exposed to it.

By the end of the first millennium, the Chinese had developed a way to prevent people from getting smallpox. They crushed smallpox scabs into a powder and inhaled it through the nose. This deliberate exposure to smallpox was less dangerous than catching the disease and offered protection from it. Similar techniques of exposure were also used in India and Turkey.

Inhaling smallpox scabs wasn't a perfect method of preventing the disease. Some people became sick from it. Over the years the practice evolved. Rather than snorting the smallpox virus, people began placing it in an open cut. They also figured out that scabs from people with mild smallpox were the safest to use.

This method wasn't practiced in Europe until the eighteenth century. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, the wife of England's ambassador to Turkey, became a leading advocate of the practice. She had learned of it while living in Turkey and had her own child receive the procedure. After that, the practice became more common, although some people remained reluctant to try it. Exposure to the live smallpox virus was still risky.

In 1796 an English physician and scientist named Edward Jenner developed a safer way to prevent smallpox. He had noticed that local milkmaids often got cowpox, a similar but much milder illness. After they got cowpox, they were protected from smallpox too. Jenner experimented, wondering if he could come up with a safer way to prevent smallpox. Eventually this led him to the idea of vaccination.

Vaccination uses a dead or weakened version of a virus, which is less dangerous than the live virus used in earlier procedures. After exposure to a virus, the immune system creates antibodies, substances that fight infection and prevent illness. Later, if the body sees that virus again, it will recognize it and know to make more antibodies. This is how the body develops immunity to fight diseases naturally. The weaker viruses used in vaccines get the body to make antibodies but don't make a person ill.

Jenner's smallpox vaccinations proved safe and effective. Governments quickly worked to vaccinate entire populations against smallpox. Soon the number of smallpox cases and deaths fell significantly in some parts of the world.

The knowledge gained from Jenner's method wasn't limited to smallpox. In the late 1800s, French scientist Louis Pasteur's studies of germs and disease helped him develop a vaccine for rabies. Over the century, scientists developed vaccines for other diseases as well, but progress was slow. By the 1920s scientists achieved more breakthroughs and more diseases could be prevented by vaccination, including diphtheria. In the 1950s researchers developed a vaccine for polio, a disease that had left thousands of children and adults paralyzed.

Smallpox still remained a threat despite the development of the vaccine. Throughout the first half of the twentieth century, many nations had wiped out smallpox entirely. But outbreaks still occurred in developing nations. In 1966 the World Health Organization began a project of mass vaccination to eliminate smallpox in the places where it still existed. By 1980 the illness had been completely eradicated.

Today children can receive vaccinations to protect them from different illnesses. But children aren't the only ones who have to get vaccinated. Many childhood vaccinations require more shots later in life. These shots are like a recharge for the original vaccine. Each year people of all ages get flu shots for protection against the influenza virus. The flu virus changes quickly, so scientists must create a new vaccine each year. The flu vaccine prevents over a million cases of flu each year.

Smallpox is no longer a threat to humans thanks to vaccines. However, new diseases have emerged with no treatments, cures, or vaccines available. Perhaps the lessons learned from smallpox will prevent future illnesses. While vaccines have saved millions of lives, there are still more lives to be saved.

A new Mars rover rolls across red sand in the Atacama Desert in Chile. The rover has all of the latest technology developed by NASA to aid in the study of Mars. Why are NASA scientists testing a Mars rover in South America? The Atacama Desert is one of the driest places on Earth, and one of the places most similar to Mars. It's the perfect place for scientists to practice for future expeditions to the red planet.

Humans have long been fascinated with Mars. After all, Mars is our neighbor—just one planet further from the sun than Earth. The red planet, named for the Roman god of war, has long been visible to the naked eye. But no one knew much about Mars for centuries.

In the 1500s scientists began to learn more about the stars and the solar system. They were able to calculate the position of Mars and learn about its orbit. In 1609 Italian scientist Galileo Galilei used an early telescope for a closer view of Mars.

As telescopes improved in the 1700s, so did the study of Mars. Scientists began to work out other details about the planet. Early measurements of its rotation and tilt were later proven to be nearly correct. Mars takes 24 hours and 37 minutes to complete a rotation. The planet has a tilt of around 25 degrees. Since these values are similar to Earth's, astronomers were curious. Could Mars be like Earth?

The red planet's physical features also encouraged people to believe that it was similar to Earth. Astronomers noticed light and dark areas on the planet's surface and believed them to be oceans and landmasses. In 1877 Giovanni Schiaparelli published a detailed map of Mars that included these Earth-like features. He also included long straight lines that he had observed cutting across Mars' landmass. These lines looked much too orderly to be natural features. Schiaparelli thought that they were waterways that had been made by intelligent life. His beliefs were disputed, and it was later realized that the lines were an optical illusion. But the idea of a complex civilization on Mars had already gripped people's imaginations.

Schiaparelli's mistaken belief helped give the word "Martian" a new meaning. It had long been an adjective that meant "having to do with Mars." Now it came to be a noun, meaning an inhabitant of Mars. By the end of the nineteenth century, novels and stories about Martians were popular. But their depictions weren't always positive. In The War of the Worlds , a novel by British author H. G. Wells, England is invaded by Martians. An adaptation of Wells' novel was broadcast on the radio in 1938. The first part of the story was told as a series of news reports. Many listeners panicked because they thought Martians had really invaded Earth.

By the 1960s the widespread belief in Martians began to disappear, but Martians remained figures in popular culture. Rather than scary unknown invaders, they were more likely to appear as funny characters in comedies. What caused humans to change their minds about Martians? Space exploration was finally possible, and humans eagerly raced to explore space.

The Soviet Union and the United States sent spacecraft to fly close to Mars and take photographs. In the 1970s, probes landed on Mars and sent back the first photographs from the surface. Mars was found to be cold and dry, with a surface covered in red dust. There were no signs of Martians. Since then, many unmanned missions have been sent to explore the red planet.

There are some similarities between Mars and Earth: Mars has polar ice caps, mountains, plains, and sand dunes. But the environment is not very Earth-like at all. The planet's atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide. With these conditions, no form of Earth life is possible on Mars. However, scientists have found the minerals and chemicals necessary for life. There is also evidence that Mars once contained water. New questions began to arise: Was there once life on Mars? Do microscopic forms of life still live deep under the surface of Mars? Might we be able to build human colonies on Mars one day? Some people even wonder if Mars could be transformed into a planet like Earth.

So far Mars has turned out to be less like Earth than early astronomers believed. But we have a long way to go before we fully understand the red planet. Luckily, more missions to Mars are planned, and the unique conditions of the Atacama Desert are helping scientists to prepare for these expeditions. Each expedition uncovers new information about Mars, but humans have barely even scratched the surface of the red planet's mysteries.

Zak and Alma waited in line at the ice cream vendor's cart. They were taking a break from racing around the park playing Dragons Search on their cell phones. They'd spent two hours trying to see who could find and capture the most dragons in the game.
"You might have the higher score now, but I'm going to win," Zak teased.
"I doubt that." Alma smiled. "There's no way you can catch up to my score!"
While Zak ordered, Alma noticed a man who looked familiar. The man was circling around, staring at his phone. "Is that our social studies teacher from last year, Mr. Perry?" she asked.
Zak nodded as he paid for the ice cream. "Hey, Mr. Perry!" he called. "Phone away or it's mine for the day!" Mr. Perry used to say that when he caught students using their phones in school.
Mr. Perry looked up and smiled. "Hi, kids. I guess you caught me!"
"I thought you didn't like cell phones," Alma said.
"Not in school," Mr. Perry replied. "But I'm thinking I might use them to teach my next unit on reading different types of maps."
"You mean, like using a map app?" Zak asked.
"Actually, there's a new game all the kids are playing," Mr. Perry explained. "You have to capture dragons and—"
"You mean Dragons Search ?" Alma asked, showing him her phone.
"That's it!" Mr. Perry said. "The game uses the Global Positioning System, or GPS. That's how the game knows where you're located and which dragons you can catch."
"I know the game uses our location," Zak said. "But I don't understand how GPS works."

"I'm sure you're not alone in that," Mr. Perry said. "GPS relies on satellites twenty-thousand kilometers above Earth. The satellites orbit Earth, and at any given time or place, there are around nine satellites overhead."
"But how does my phone communicate with them?" Alma asked.
"The satellites regularly send signals with their position. The GPS receivers in our devices pick up those signals," Mr. Perry said.
"Twenty-thousand kilometers above Earth!" Alma exclaimed. "It must take a long time for the signals to reach Earth."

"Nope! The signals travel very fast—at the speed of light," Mr. Perry replied. "Your device calculates the distance between the satellites to find the exact longitude and latitude of your location. The GPS receiver needs at least three satellite signals to calculate your position."
"With so many satellites up in space, how do they know not to bump into each other?" Zak asked.

"Good question," Mr. Perry said. "The satellites travel in a fixed orbit around Earth at a set rate of speed. The satellites and orbits are spaced to maintain a safe distance from each other. Each satellite takes approximately 12 hours to complete one orbit."
"My cousins have a hobby they're always talking about," Zak said. "It has something to do with GPS. It starts with 'geo.'"
"Geocaching?" Mr. Perry asked.
"That's it!" Zak licked some ice cream as it started dripping.
"Geocaching is like a giant treasure hunt," Mr. Perry explained. "It's become very popular—there are over one million geocaches hidden all over the world."
"How do you play?" Alma asked.
"Players choose a geocache from a list. Then, using the geocache's coordinates, they use GPS to find the geocache. It usually involves a fun hike or exploring an interesting neighborhood."
"Sounds like Dragons Search ," Alma said.

"Kind of. Except geocaches are real boxes with real objects inside," Mr. Perry explained. "If you take something out of the box, you leave something of similar value behind. You also sign the logbook, leaving a note for other geocachers."
"We should ask your cousins to take us geocaching, Zak," Alma said.
"Just remember to be respectful and safe. Don't roam onto private property or into dangerous terrain. And don't take unnecessary risks just to reach the geocache," Mr. Perry said.
"Thanks for the lesson, Mr. Perry," Zak said. "When we get back to our game, I'm going to imagine signals bouncing between my phone and the GPS satellites."
"Me too," Alma laughed. "That'll make beating Zak even more fun!"
Skyler surveyed the clean beach and let out a sigh of relief. Even somber Walter showed a hint of a smile.

Skyler had helped to organize a beach cleanup for her school's Green Club. She had only recently joined the club, after gaining an interest in environmental issues, and eagerly volunteered to help plan the effort. The Green Club had teamed up with a local private school for the first time. Skyler was definitely impressed by Walter, the president of the private school's environmental club. Walter had not only gotten plastic utensils and straws banned from his school's cafeteria, but he'd also gotten the two schools together. But there was one thing about working with Walter that was challenging—he was always so serious!
"This is going to look great for our yearbook," Skyler said excitedly, snapping a picture of the beach. "It was a long morning, but we cleaned up the entire beach! Now it looks almost pristine."
"We did a lot of work, but there's still plastic all around," Walter said.

"Huh?" Skyler furrowed her brow. The students had collected a huge amount of plastic debris—wrappers, bottles, and bags. Club members were now carefully combing through it, checking to see what was recyclable and what was not. "I don't see anymore plastic," she mumbled.
"You might not see it, but that doesn't mean it's not there," Walter said. "Haven't you heard of microplastics?"
"Oh!" Skyler said. "I've heard of microplastics, but I don't really know much about them."

"Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic less than five millimeters in size. Looking at the beach now, it's not obvious that it's still polluted with plastic. That's because microplastics are so tiny."
"Where do microplastics come from?" Skyler asked.

"They come from nearly anything that has plastic," Walter said. "Even though plastic may take hundreds of years to break down—which is why we need to lessen our consumption—it still breaks down. And when it does, tiny fragments are released into the water, soil, and air."
"Air?"

"Yeah. Microplastics are even in the air, which means we breathe them in. Since the particles are so small, they can easily travel through the air like dust. Or they come from synthetic fibers like polyester that get shed from clothes. These fibers also enter the water when we do laundry." Walter sighed. "Did you know that microplastics are in the food chain too?"
Skyler shook her head.

"A lot of microplastics get consumed by seafood," Walter continued. "Small sea animals ingest microplastics, then larger fish eat them. And then we eat those fish! What's worse is that the chemicals used to make plastic can be toxic and even cause cancer. All this stuff ends up in our bodies."
"I thought I knew a lot about saving the planet," Skyler said, "but I guess there's still a lot to learn."
Walter nodded. "Microplastics aren't new, but our understanding of them is. And many people still don't see how prevalent the problem really is."
"I wonder what can be done," Skyler said.

"Well, cleaning up the beach was a good thing to do," Walter said. "It will prevent some microplastics from contaminating the beach. We should all recycle, of course, and try to use less plastic. Or, we can use biodegradable plastic instead. New plastics are being made out of biodegradable materials."

"But they might not be as biodegradable as we think, and some use more materials to make than regular plastics," Skyler said. "It's also easier for wealthy people to use less plastic or buy different products, but not everyone can afford to do that. Green products are usually more expensive. It's hard to tell people to use less plastic when the alternatives are too expensive for them."
"Right, and some products labeled 'green' aren't really green at all. Companies just use green packaging or earth-friendly words to sell things at higher prices."
"That's called greenwashing."

Walter nodded. "Yeah. I convinced my mom to use new floor wipes because the box looked eco-friendly. But later I read that they weren't any different from the other wipes. That made me mad." He shook his head. "Saving the earth is the right thing for all of us to do. But lots of corporations treat it as a way to make more money."
"Our planet is running out of time," Skyler said. "I hope we can find some solutions before it's too late."

Walter glanced up at the other kids who were still busy sorting plastic. "There aren't any easy solutions. But you and I have joined these clubs, and today's project will make a difference. And right now there's something else we can do." Walter grinned. "Help the other kids! They probably think we're slacking off!"
Skyler smiled back, pleased to see Walter lightening up. As they headed toward the group of students, Walter suddenly stopped. "Maybe our school clubs can collaborate more often," he said.
Skyler's smile widened. "Great idea!"

Animals are amazing! Some animals can breathe underwater. Some have protective skeletons on the outside of their bodies. A few can even regrow lost limbs! Animals can do these things thanks to their bodies. Humans can't do any of these things, but wouldn't it be great if we could? Imagining humans with these features brings up some incredible questions.

Fish can live underwater because they have gills that take oxygen from water. What if humans had gills? We could swim all day without having to surface for a breath. Why haven't humans evolved gills? It would be so convenient! Or maybe not.

All mammals, including humans, are warm-blooded. This means they produce their own heat to keep themselves warm and regulate their body temperature. This takes a lot of oxygen. Fish don't need much oxygen. They are cold-blooded. Their body temperature changes depending on the surrounding temperature.

A human's lungs are much larger than a fish's gills because humans need more oxygen to create body heat. Gills aren't meant for this. If humans had gills large enough to provide the oxygen we need, they would be enormous. Our bodies would look completely different! Gills are better for smaller, cold-blooded creatures.

Another cool animal feature is the exoskeleton. That's a skeleton on the outside of the body. Insects, spiders, and crustaceans have them. It's not a rare feature at all. More than 80 percent of all animals on earth have exoskeletons. So why not humans? Built-in armor would certainly look cool! But it might not work as well for humans as it does for tarantulas or lobsters.

Like gills, exoskeletons are best suited to small creatures. An exoskeleton has to be light enough for a creature to carry. And it has to provide the creature with protection. A human, of course, is much larger than a shrimp. Even a thin exoskeleton would be far too heavy for us to carry around. This is one of the challenges the military faces when designing exoskeleton armor. It's hard to find materials that are super light but also strong.

An exoskeleton might not even offer a human much protection. Animals that have exoskeletons go through a process called molting. This is when they shed their old skeletons to grow new ones. During molting, an animal is left with no protection. Luckily their new, small exoskeletons grow pretty quickly. But it would take a human much longer to grow a new skeleton than it would take a small crab. All that time the person would be in danger—and unable to stand up. After all, during molting, we wouldn't have a skeleton to support our muscles.

Not all animal kingdom adaptations would be impractical for humans. Some animals, like starfish, have the ability to regenerate lost limbs. This really would be useful since losing a limb can be a major challenge.

Humans can already grow new blood cells, skin, and muscle. But no mammal can regrow an entire lost limb. Scientists aren't sure why. It may have something to do with scars. When a body part is injured, the body produces chemicals that help prevent infection. Those chemicals also cause scars. Starfish don't get scars—they just grow new limbs. But human cells are programmed to only grow in a controlled way. Cancer is a disease that occurs from cells that grow uncontrollably.
Scientists don't think regrowing limbs is completely impossible. In fact, they are making progress in learning to grow human body parts. With luck, this animal what-if might one day be real.

Animals can do many things that humans can't do. But our bodies let us do some incredible things that animals can't do. Because of the structure of our bodies, we can talk and communicate in ways that animals can't. We're the only animal that walks upright all the time. Our hands are more flexible and useful than other animals' hands. Thanks to the complexity of our brains, we can figure out how cells work. And best of all, we can imagine what-ifs! Animals definitely can't do that!

Today most supermarkets have large frozen food sections. Freezer cases are stocked with a variety of convenient meals that can be cooked in minutes. But frozen foods weren't always common—or widely eaten. It took innovations, war, and clever marketing to convince consumers to give frozen foods a try.

From 1912 to 1915, an American named Clarence Birdseye worked in Labrador, a region in northeastern Canada. People there often froze food to preserve it. Birdseye noticed how good frozen fish tasted in Labrador. When thawed, it tasted as delicious as freshly caught fish. But in the United States, frozen food was awful. After being cooked, it became mushy and bland. Intrigued by this difference, Birdseye decided to investigate.

Birdseye eventually discovered that melting ice crystals were the reason frozen food became mushy. In Labrador, temperatures could dip to -30 degrees Celsius. At that temperature, fish froze as soon as they were pulled from the water and exposed to frigid air. Since the food froze so quickly, only small ice crystals formed, which didn't affect the food much. In the United States, foods were frozen gradually and at higher temperatures than in Labrador. This created large ice crystals—and the problems with taste.

To prevent ice crystals from forming, Birdseye developed flash freezing—a way to freeze food quickly in a factory. This new method, available by the 1920s, recreated the way food was frozen in Labrador.

Flash freezing improved the taste of frozen foods, but it didn't make an immediate difference to consumers. For one thing, most homes didn't have freezers. For another, there was already a popular way to preserve food without a freezer: canning.

It wasn't until the 1940s that circumstances created a true market for frozen foods. During World War II, canned foods were sent to war fronts to feed soldiers. At home, civilians were encouraged to buy more frozen food. With men off fighting the war, many women were joining the workforce, filling jobs that men had left behind. These busy working women, who had to work and prepare meals for their families, discovered they liked the ease of serving frozen foods.

After the war, freezers became more available, and frozen food was here to stay. Although convenient, frozen foods were still limited to single ingredients like fruits or vegetables. They were frozen raw, and the consumer had to thaw and then fully cook them.

In 1953 an executive with Swanson Foods had an idea to change that. After seeing some metal meal trays on an airplane, he wanted to try freezing a full dinner—turkey with gravy, potatoes, and peas. A company called Maxson Food Systems had already developed frozen meals to be served on transatlantic military flights. Maxson had also tried to sell these meals to regular consumers, but with little success. Swanson Foods thought it could succeed where Maxson had failed.

But it wasn't easy to get an entire meal to cook in one tray at the same time and temperature. Each part of the meal required a different cooking time. Swanson solved this problem by cooking each part separately. Then each item was placed into the tray, and the tray was frozen, packaged, and sold. A consumer could bake the tray in the oven for about 25 minutes. The meal would defrost, finish cooking, and be ready to eat.

The next challenge was convincing consumers to buy the frozen meals. Another new technology helped Swanson sell its new product: the TV set. Just like freezers, TVs were now in most American homes. So Swanson sold its new product in a colorful box that looked like a television set. Swanson called these meals TV dinners. Not surprisingly, advertisements showed families eating these quick-to-prepare meals while they watched TV.
New technologies, changing society, and clever advertising all worked well for Swanson. Soon TV dinners were a huge hit with American families.

In the 1980s, as microwaves began to appear in more home kitchens, manufacturers of frozen meals had to adapt again. The trays switched from metal to plastic, and the cooking times were reduced to minutes. By then, people's lives had changed too, and they were busier than ever. Instead of sit-down meals, new frozen foods appeared that were meant to be eaten on the go, like pocket sandwiches and burritos. Companies later introduced healthy options and international dishes to appeal to the changing needs and tastes of consumers.

Frozen meals have changed a lot since Swanson's first TV dinners. Yet people still appreciate the convenience of frozen foods. What will the next frozen food innovation be? And how will technology change our future eating habits?

Farming might not seem like a high-tech business. Farmers plant seeds, water them, and let the plants grow. Then the crops are harvested, and the food eventually gets to our tables. But thanks to genetic engineering, farming has become high-tech. With genetic engineering, scientists can change the genes of living things. This technology lets scientists create plants and animals that better meet the needs of humans.

Genes control the characteristics of living things, determining features such as color, size, and appearance. Scientists have learned a lot about modifying genes in recent years. But humans have actually been modifying plants and animals for much longer. Early cultures bred animals with useful traits, hoping the animals' offspring would inherit these traits. This process is called selective breeding. Using it, humans produced stronger and faster horses, as well as sheep with more wool. Selective breeding also created new types of fruits and vegetables. Even many popular dog breeds are the product of selective breeding.

Selective breeding works well, but it's slow and limited. Modern genetic engineering is faster and lets scientists achieve many more results. Scientists can change a species' characteristics by editing its genes. This can mean deleting genes that control unwanted characteristics or transferring genes from another species. An organism, or living thing, that is modified this way is known as a GMO. GMO stands for genetically modified organism.

GMOs can be used to help the environment. For example, scientists are working on modifying pigs to produce less pollution from their poop. Another GMO is a tree modified for papermaking. Making paper from this tree requires fewer chemicals and less energy.

Genetic engineering is a big help to farmers growing crops for food as well. Scientists have found a way to protect bananas from a deadly disease by using a gene found in green peppers. This gene protects the peppers from the disease. Scientists can transfer the gene to bananas. The modified bananas are then resistant to the disease.

GMO crops can also be made resistant to insects. Farmers don't have to use as many pesticides with these crops. This is a big advantage for farmers who can't afford pesticides. It also lets farmers avoid using dangerous chemicals. And that keeps more chemicals out of the environment.

In many places in the world, water is limited. Scientists can create GMO crops that need less water. Other crops can be designed to produce more food on less land. This could help feed the world's growing population without using more land.

GMOs have health benefits as well. Scientists have engineered beef cattle that are resistant to disease. Other foods can be engineered to have more nutrients. And GMOs can even be used to make medicines more effective and less expensive.
With genetic engineering, many things can be improved and the possibilities are endless. All scientists need are the right genes to make longer-lasting, better-tasting, and more nutritious foods.

This sounds like great news, but genetic engineering is still a new technology. Its consequences aren't completely understood. GMOs could pose risks. People might develop allergies to GMO foods. GMOs themselves could also show unexpected results. They could grow faster or slower, or differently than expected. GMO crops could spread their genes to other plants in the wild. This could cause changes in the environment.

Many people are opposed to GMOs for these reasons. Some countries have completely banned them, while others have laws that control their use. In many places GMOs must be clearly labeled. Even in countries where they are allowed, local governments sometimes write laws to ban them.

Many people will only buy food labeled non-GMO. These people often oppose GMOs for reasons beyond safety. Some believe it is wrong for humans to change nature in this way. Or they worry that companies who own GMOs will have too much control over the world's food supply.

So far the GMOs that have been developed seem safe. GMOs have the potential to be a great benefit to humans. But they also have the potential to create future problems. There is still a long way to go before the technology and its effects are fully understood.

Whoosh! Snow sprayed as Kai swerved around a tree. His skis carved two neat lines down the trail. It was only an intermediate trail, but it was more difficult than the intermediate trails Kai skied back home in Vermont. When he reached the bottom, he found his best friend, Zinnia, waiting for him.
"She beat me again!" Kai thought. He didn't let that bother him though. Zinnia's aunt and uncle owned the ski resort, so it made sense that she was an accomplished skier.
"You call that an intermediate trail?" Kai said. "That was hard!"

Zinnia laughed. "Every ski resort has its own rating system. That was an intermediate trail only compared to the other trails at this resort. Plus, you're used to Vermont's smaller mountains. We're in Colorado now."
"Right," Kai said. "These mountains are huge!"
"Come on," Zinnia said, taking off. "Let's check out a more advanced slope—Cliffhanger!"
Kai gulped. "The intermediate trail was already hard," he thought. "Cliffhanger will probably be way more intense than the advanced slopes that I'm used to back home!"
Kai and Zinnia rode the chairlift up the mountain. When they got to the top, Kai was a little disappointed, but also relieved—Cliffhanger was closed for maintenance.
"Hey, Zinnia!" A woman walked toward them.
"Hi, Aunt Kate!" Zinnia said before introducing Kai to her aunt.
"Sorry about Cliffhanger," Aunt Kate said. "It's closed for grooming right now."
Kai was confused. "Grooming?"

Aunt Kate smiled. "That's what we call it when we get trails ready for skiers. We usually do it at night, but last night was too busy. Our top priority is always getting the easier trails groomed first. Fewer people use the advanced trails, so we don't usually bother with them, but they've gotten pretty icy."
Kai looked down the slope and saw machines blowing out thick, powdery white clouds. "What do those machines do?"
"They're making artificial snow," Aunt Kate said.
"Artificial? Man-made snow?" Kai blinked. "What's it made out of?"
"It's still just frozen water, like real snow," Zinnia said.

"The ski resort can only earn money a few months each year," Aunt Kate explained, "and some winters we don't get enough snowfall. We can't afford to close down while we wait for more snow to fall. So we make our own."
"How do the snowmakers work?" Kai asked.

"The process starts with water," Aunt Kate said. "A special protein that helps ice crystals form is added to the water, which is then pumped up to the machines. Each machine has several nozzles that shoot water, along with compressed air, into a large fan. The mixture of water and air sprays out of the fan, freezes, and then falls as snow."
Kai saw a couple of large red vehicles pushing snow downhill.
"Those are our snowcats," Aunt Kate said. "They groom the slopes by pushing snow into place and smoothing it out, creating a perfect surface for skiers."
"So you can have snow any time of year?" Kai asked.

"Not exactly," Aunt Kate said. "The temperature still needs to be around freezing for the machines to work properly and efficiently. But as long as the air isn't too humid, we can make snow even when it’s too warm for snow to fall naturally. If it's too humid, the water won't freeze. Artificial snow has even been used in the Winter Olympics since 1980. The majority of the snow used in the Winter Olympics in Sochi and Pyeongchang was man-made."

"Artificial snow makes a better surface for winter sports," Zinnia said. "It's more durable and consistent than real snow—it doesn't clump together. Plus, without artificial snow, we wouldn't be able to go skiing all winter long."

"Not only that," Aunt Kate added, "we wouldn't be able to pay our employees' wages. The town's economy depends on us. We don't just have people grooming the slopes and operating the snowmakers. We also hire people to operate chairlifts, monitor the slopes, and provide skiing and snowboarding lessons."
"Hey!" Zinnia said. "Where are the snowcats going?"
Kai looked down and saw the vehicles driving farther down the mountain.
"They're finished grooming Cliffhanger," Aunt Kate said. "You two have fun. I'll see you later!"
Zinnia looked at Kai and grinned. "Ready for your first really big thrill here in Colorado?"
Kai looked down the slope again. Part of him wished Cliffhanger was still closed—then he wouldn't have to ski down it. But another part of him was excited.
Kai adjusted his ski goggles. "Let's do it!"

As long as people have been able to communicate, they have used codes to pass secret information to their friends and allies. From the battlefields of ancient Sparta to the modern Internet, codes and ciphers have proved essential when security is at stake. Cryptography—from the Greek words kryptos , meaning "hidden," and graphos , meaning "writing"—is the art of converting a message from its original form into one that hides its meaning. The encrypted message is supposed to be understood only by its author and its intended recipient, who knows how to read it. Humans have found ingenious ways not only to create and transmit secret communications, but to intercept and decipher them as well.

In order to communicate secretly, people have tried to conceal the very existence of their messages. For example, the ancient Greeks commonly used wax-covered wooden tablets to write on, scratching words into the wax. They would reuse them by simply melting new layers of wax onto the tablets. To keep something secret, they would write a message on the bare wood tablet and only then cover it with wax to make it look unused. When the tablet reached its destination, the recipient would melt the wax off to see the information hidden underneath. A Greek general relayed a message to an ally using a different technique: he shaved the head of a trusted slave and tattooed the information onto his head. After his hair grew out, the message was completely hidden, and the slave was sent to deliver it. Messages sent through methods like these, however, were easily intercepted if someone found out about their presence, so other ways to communicate in secrecy were developed.

One of the first documented uses of a cipher was by Hebrew scribes in the ancient Middle East. As early as 600 BC, these scribes encrypted parts of their texts by using the "Atbash cipher," in which they replaced the first letter of the alphabet with the last letter, the second with the second to last, and so on. In the English version of the Atbash cipher, the letter a would instead appear as z . This simple process made text unreadable to anyone who did not have the key—in this case, the fact that the alphabet was reversed.

By 500 BC, the Spartans of Greece were using cryptography on the battlefield. They passed messages with a scytale, a thin strip of leather wound tightly around a wooden stick. The secret message was written across the leather after it was wrapped around the stick, from one end of the stick to the other. The leather strip was then unwound, removed from the wood, and carried to its destination—as something as innocent as a belt, for instance. The recipient of the strip would then wind it around another stick of identical size. The letters that formed the message would line up once again, and the message could easily be read; if the stick was not the right size, the text would be incomprehensible.

Several hundred years later, Julius Caesar also used a cipher during his many military campaigns to keep his messages secret. For each letter of the message, he substituted the one that appears three letters later in the alphabet. So the letter a would be replaced with d, b with e , and so on. Although the Caesar cipher is simple by today’s standards, it gave Caesar a great strategic advantage.

The Middle Ages and Renaissance saw a rapid rise in cryptography. The ability to communicate secretly became a priority not only of military commanders, but also of kings and bishops. In the fifteenth century, Leon Battista Alberti, an Italian architect, made a breakthrough in cryptography when he placed together two metal disks—one smaller, one larger—with the alphabet printed on each. The letters of the alphabet on the outer disk were in the correct order, while the letters on the inner circle were mixed up. A key indicated how to line up the disks—for instance, the message sender and its recipient would agree to rotate the inner disk to match its letter c with the letter a on the outer disk. Then, based on the pairings of the letters with the disks in that position, the message could easily be converted into the cipher and back again.

Although many mechanical devices were designed for use by cryptographers, few major advances were made in cryptography until the nineteenth century. During the 1830s, Samuel Morse invented a new telegraph and Morse code, a system to encode letters into combinations of dots and dashes. This allowed messages to be tapped out and transmitted over wires in the form of short and long tones.

By the beginning of the twentieth century, cryptography was routinely used by governments around the world. The telegraph machine had given way to radio, and the battle to create new methods of encryption intensified, because for every code invented, people known as "code breakers" worked tirelessly to solve the riddle. Governments created special departments to create new ciphers, as well as to intercept and decipher others' secret communications. As World War I loomed in Europe, the ability of nations to send and receive encrypted messages freely was crucial. Portable "cipher machines" first came into use at this time; they enabled military commanders to communicate with their headquarters quickly and securely, even from remote locations. Amid the chaos of the battlefield, the cipher machines had to be protected at all costs. If they fell into enemy hands, information might be revealed that would forever alter the course of events, as history has shown.

During World War II, the ability to decipher encrypted communications proved instrumental. The United States won the critical Battle of Midway against the Japanese after breaking the code used by Japan's military. England was able to prepare for and withstand the Germans' air and submarine attacks because the British had broken the ciphers created by the German Enigma machine. The Enigma was so important that, in order to hide the fact it had been broken, England resorted to other explanations for its ability to resist the Germans' assaults.

Since World War II, the science of encryption has taken a giant leap forward. The introduction of computers has made codes and ciphers both easier to create and to break. As a result, a whole industry has risen to provide for people's security needs. Today, cryptography is a common part of most people's daily lives, whether they know it or not. Whenever people enter a password on the Internet or punch a PIN (personal identification number) into an ATM, they are using a secret code. Every email message is encrypted after it leaves the computer and deciphered when it arrives at its destination. Hackers—people who try to break into the computer systems of governments or corporations—are actually attempting to break the codes used to write software.

The desire for secrecy has been a part of human nature for thousands of years, and as humans have evolved, so has the art of concealing information. As electronic communication becomes an even greater part of our lives, new, tougher codes will be developed, and the importance of cryptography will continue to increase for future generations.

In 1868, John Muir traveled to the Yosemite Valley in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California. When he saw it, he wrote, "No temple made with human hands can compare with Yosemite." Muir was a pioneer in the science of ecology—the study of living things and their environments. He was also one of the first people to promote "ecotourism"—a combination of "ecology" and "tourism." In 1892, he founded an environmental organization called the Sierra Club, with the following motto: "Explore, enjoy, and protect the planet." Muir knew how important natural wonders were to the human spirit, and he encouraged the government to protect untouched areas for future generations. But careless people can damage the wilderness they wish to experience. In Muir's beloved Yosemite, for instance, the enormous Wawona Tree was nearly two thousand years old when a tunnel big enough for a car was cut through its trunk. The tree died not even a century later; the weakened trunk couldn't support the weight of the snow on its branches after a storm in 1969.

Since the Wawona Tree fell, however, many people have realized the impact their travels can have on the environment. Although tourism has existed ever since people have had free time and money to spend, during the 1980s, the idea of ecotourism finally took hold. Its goals are to provide experiences in nature that educate the public, protect the environment, and ensure the prosperity of indigenous people. Ecologists felt that if people had a better understanding of the planet, they would work harder to protect it. They encouraged activities that allow people to learn about a variety of ecosystems and experience wildlife up close—without damaging the environment.

Before ecotourism, many tourists would flock to interesting or relaxing places without a thought about the consequences of their actions. For example, Cancún Island, a narrow strip of land off the eastern coast of Mexico, served as a nesting site for sea turtles and seabirds. But in the 1970s, a resort was built to attract vacationers. Roads and golf courses followed, and soon, luxury hotels lined the beach. Crowds packed the resort area, seriously affecting the island's environment. Garbage piled up, sewage and chemicals contaminated the local lagoon, and sunscreen from the bodies of thousands of swimmers began to destroy the nearby coral reef.

Ecotourism, on the other hand, offers some exciting alternatives to lying on a beach with thousands of other vacationers. Ecotourists can experience the wilderness and help maintain it by clearing old hiking trails while nature guides lead them through the forest. Working and camping on the trails, visitors learn firsthand what the slogan "Leave nothing but footprints, take nothing but photographs" really means. Rafting is another great way to interact with nature while leaving no trace on the river ecosystem, and because no motor is used, rafting conserves energy too.

Ecotourists can also learn about the environment and help to preserve fragile ecosystems by visiting the world's rain forests. The Central American country of Costa Rica, for example, features trams and walkways suspended in the jungle's canopy. Visitors can ride or walk among the treetops and see birds, large mammals, and plants that collect water for the creatures living high in the trees. The money generated by vacationers supports rain-forest conservation and allows activists to fight deforestation.

Travelers looking for adventure can experience Africa's biodiversity and contribute to protecting its wildlife. While tracking gorillas in the jungles of Rwanda, tourists can also catch sight of lions and elephants. Ecotourism companies hire indigenous people to act as guides for the tourists. When locals make an income by guiding and educating tourists attracted by the wildlife, the members of the community are more likely to protect the habitat and less likely to resort to poaching.

To get a unique view of the Central Serengeti in Tanzania, visitors can fly above the African plain in a hot-air balloon. The largest wildlife migration in the world takes place here, so this is the only place on the planet visitors can witness herds of thousands of wildebeests and zebras passing in search of new pastures. Most people would say shooting a photograph on a safari is much better than shooting an animal. These sightseeing safaris have become a booming business for local tour operators, and the money the tourists bring in helps maintain the natural beauty of the area.

The tourism industry has taken notice that as people become more environmentally conscious, they are willing to pay higher prices to vacation at "green" resorts. These places make the environment a priority. They try to use renewable resources, to conserve water, and to minimize their "carbon footprint"—the amount of greenhouse gases they produce. They may do this by using materials that can be replenished quickly, such as bamboo, instead of trees that take longer to grow back. Or they may use less water by giving guests the option of having their towels and sheets laundered every few days instead of daily. These practices also allow businesses to lower their energy consumption. By lessening their impact on the environment, resort owners can also increase their profits. Not only do their costs decrease, but green practices attract greater numbers of guests.

Some unethical companies, however, take advantage of the public's willingness to spend a little extra to protect the planet. These companies mislead consumers by claiming to be green, even though their concern for the environment takes a back seat to their desire for profits. This is called "greenwashing." For example, in 2002, nature tourists paid to travel to a beach on the west coast of Africa to see sea turtles laying their eggs. Local activists watched with horror as the visitors drove along the beach on all-terrain vehicles, running over nests and rushing right up to the turtles. A spokeswoman for the International Fund for Animal Welfare criticized the tour's organizers, saying, "It was completely irresponsible. They didn't care about the animals."

Many people do not understand the magnitude of humans' effect on sensitive habitats. But some people are aware of the dangers and are anxious to see the frontiers that are disappearing. On vacation, they travel to faraway places like Antarctica or Australia's Great Barrier Reef to see them before they become damaged beyond repair by global warming. Unfortunately, these trips often add to the problem. For instance, airplanes release large amounts of greenhouse gases and make global warming worse.

Ecotourism has been a double-edged sword for the environment. On one hand, it has provided much-needed funds for the protection of endangered species and at-risk areas while educating the public. On the other hand, ecotourism has created a stampede into vulnerable areas of the world, hastening the destruction of many of these precious sites. Many hope that in the future, ecotourism will create even more chances for people to learn about nature, but in a more responsible way. Because the more people recognize how connected they are to the natural world, the more determined they will be to protect it.

Parents have known for thousands of years that physical characteristics—such as curly hair or brown eyes—seem to run in the family. These characteristics are called inherited traits, and the transmission of traits from generation to generation is called heredity. Farmers realized the power of inherited traits very early on—thousands of years ago, when plants were first being cultivated and animals were first being domesticated. When selecting individuals to breed, a farmer would choose the stock with the best traits—the strongest oxen, the fastest horses, or the plants with the largest fruit—in the hope that their offspring would have the same characteristics.

By the nineteenth century, it still wasn't known exactly how those traits were passed from one generation to another. Gregor Mendel, now known as the father of genetics, studied the hereditary patterns of pea plants. Starting in 1856, he spent years performing experiments and observing traits like flower color, seed shape, and stem length. For example, Mendel bred a pea plant that produced only green peas with another that produced only yellow peas. By doing this, he created a hybrid generation of pea plants, one that produced only yellow peas. Then he took some of those hybrid plants and bred them with each other. The green trait reappeared in approximately a quarter of the peas in the next generation. This showed Mendel that individuals can pass a characteristic to the next generation even if they do not express that trait. These observations led Mendel to conclude that every trait is controlled by "factors." Each individual receives two of these factors for each trait—one version from each parent. Sometimes, one version is expressed, and at other times, the other version is expressed.

Meanwhile, British scientist Charles Darwin had also been observing traits and experimenting. Darwin was puzzled by physical variations that had been absent in previous generations but suddenly appeared in a new generation of an organism. He proposed that the characteristics of a species change over time through a process he called "natural selection." Individuals that are not well adapted to their environment die young and do not have a chance to reproduce. Other individuals are better adapted, with features that make them more competitive in the struggle for survival and mates. These features are known as adaptations. Darwin observed examples of adaptation in a group of birds known now as Darwin's finches. Originally all one species, the finches had spread to different islands within the Galapagos Archipelago. Over time, the beaks of these finches changed, becoming suited to whatever food was available in each area. As a result, the one species had branched out into 14 species. Darwin’s great insight—that over many generations, species can change dramatically to better fit their environments—is known as the theory of evolution. He published his ideas in 1859 in a groundbreaking book called On the Origin of Species . But Darwin still did not understand the biology behind this process.

The modern science of heredity is known as genetics. In the decades following the work of Mendel and Darwin, scientists continued to study heredity. By the 1940s, scientists had deduced that at the center of the puzzle is a molecule that they called deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). DNA contains the biological set of instructions that make each species unique. What makes an elephant an elephant? DNA. What makes a tulip a tulip? DNA. Minor changes in DNA, called mutations, lead to changes in the structure and behavior of organisms and, over millions and millions of years, lead to new and different life forms. This is the process behind Darwin's theory of evolution.

Although researchers were relatively sure that DNA was the key to inherited traits, they didn't know what it looked like. In 1953, the scientific community was racing to discover its structure. One team, at Cambridge University, was led by James Watson and Francis Crick. Researchers Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin, at King's College in London, were also working on the problem. Franklin used x-rays to make images of a DNA sample, and she suspected that the structure was a helix shape. Her partner showed Franklin's research to Watson and Crick. The Cambridge team solved the rest of the puzzle. DNA was helix-shaped, but it was a double helix—a double-stranded, twisted molecule. This discovery won Watson, Crick, and Wilkins the 1962 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine. (Franklin had died of illness in 1958.) The work of these two teams allowed other scientists to unravel the mystery of DNA.

DNA is found in the nucleus of every cell. It is organized into structures called chromosomes. Chromosomes are made up of genes. Human chromosomes have tens of thousands of genes, and all of these genes together—known as a genome—control an organism's characteristics.

Further discoveries in the twentieth century paved the way for amazing advances in genetics. In the 1970s, "genetic engineering" became possible. Scientists learned how to take a gene from one organism and combine it with the DNA of another. For example, a gene that keeps flounder from freezing in cold water was cut from the chromosome of the fish and inserted into a tomato's DNA. This change resulted in a tomato less vulnerable to frost. Genes have been inserted into many other crops to make the plants resistant to disease or to increase production. Although genetically modified crops are becoming quite common, many believe that they pose a significant danger to the environment and human health because their long-term effects are not known.

Promising—and somewhat less controversial—advances have also been made in the area of human genetics. In the 1980s, scientists developed methods to compare the DNA sequence of different individuals. DNA left behind at the scene of a crime has been used as evidence in court, both to prosecute criminals and to set free people who have been wrongly accused. DNA sequencing techniques are also useful in the field of medicine. Studying families with rare genetic disorders has allowed doctors to trace the genetic basis of disease through generations. This kind of genetic tracking helps doctors to predict the likelihood of a person getting a disease and to diagnose it—although not to cure the illness. However, some genetic diseases can now be treated by replacing damaged genes with healthy ones, a practice called gene therapy. In many cases, it's not possible or ethical to experiment on humans, so scientists often rely on other organisms, ones that reproduce rapidly such as mice or fruit flies, to learn more about the effects of gene therapy.

The twenty-first century continues to be a time of technological advancement in genetics. The first milestone of the twenty-first century was the completion of the Human Genome Project in 2003. Researchers now know the DNA sequence of all human genes, and are making a detailed map of each chromosome. Doctors are able to take a sample of a person's DNA, scan it, and determine his or her genetic risk. New mysteries and concerns will undoubtedly arise as scientists continue to explore genetics. But their discoveries will also answer many questions about the biology of the world's species and the code of life.

12.title: Diamonds: Not Just a Pretty Face

paragraphs.text: They have been called "a girl’s best friend" and "a symbol of undying love." They have been a sign of status and wealth for centuries. What are they? Diamonds, of course. But diamonds are not just "a pretty face"; they are a valuable commodity.

Diamonds are a form of carbon, but unlike other forms of carbon such as graphite (the substance used as pencil lead), diamonds are created in very unusual conditions. Scientists estimate that diamonds are formed over millennia, 150 to 670 kilometers beneath the earth’s surface, where the extremely high pressure and temperatures needed to crystallize carbon into diamond exist. Thus, they are extremely old—at minimum, millions of years old, with some as much as three billion years old. Meteorites can also create diamonds when they slam into the earth’s surface, producing in the impact the necessary temperatures of 1,000 to 1,200 degrees Celsius and extremely high pressure. Another type of diamond, black or gray opaque stones called carbonados, was created in space and carried to earth by meteorites.

Diamonds are brought from the depths of the earth to the surface in many ways. Sometimes, magma carries them upward from deep within the earth’s crust. In certain areas, magma flowing to the surface has formed tunnels, or "pipes," that include a high concentration of diamonds. These are commonly called "kimberlite pipes," after the first one discovered in Kimberley, South Africa. Most diamonds are mined from kimberlite pipes in South Africa, Russia, Australia, Botswana, and Zaire. Other methods have been created to find diamonds washed into waterways through erosion or landslides. Diamond mining, unfortunately, brings with it many environmental concerns. For instance, the chemical leftovers of the mining process are often dumped into rivers and streams, polluting the water.

Another concern within the diamond industry involves conflict diamonds, also known as blood diamonds. These are diamonds mined and sold to finance wars and violent revolutions. Blood diamonds are also linked to child slavery and child soldiers. To make it more difficult to finance war through diamond sales, the diamond industry has organized a certification system to establish that a diamond has not come from a conflict region. The system has been largely effective because De Beers, a South African company, controls more than half the worldwide supply and sales of diamonds and authorizes only a limited number of buyers to acquire diamonds.

Diamonds continue to be popular because of their extraordinary physical properties. With a rating of ten on the Mohs hardness scale, which measures the relative hardness of minerals, diamonds are the hardest known naturally occurring substance. Thus, a diamond can only be scratched by another diamond. Diamonds also rate highly in brilliance, which refers to how much light a gemstone reflects. Another property for which diamonds are noted is fire, which refers to the way light disperses into the full spectrum of colors when it passes through a gemstone. White light passing through a diamond is separated into all the colors of the rainbow. Because of these flashes of color, diamonds are said to have a very high degree of fire. The greater the brilliance and fire of a particular diamond, the greater its value.

Most people are familiar with clear diamonds, as these are most popular. Diamonds have many levels of transparency, however, and come in a wide range of colors—including green, blue, red, orange, yellow, and brown. The rarer colored diamonds are known as "fancies" and are more expensive than white diamonds.

Only the highest-quality diamonds are selected for jewelry. Diamonds are judged according to the "four Cs": color, clarity, carat, and cut. Color refers to the hue of the diamond. Colorless diamonds are sought after due to their image of purity and sophistication. Fancies that exhibit a pure color are highly esteemed and very valuable. On the other hand, diamonds with tinges of yellow are usually not used as gems at all. Clarity indicates whether there are internal blemishes or flaws in the stone. Veins or other visible imperfections will drive down the value of a diamond. Carat refers to a diamond’s mass. One carat equals two hundred milligrams. Obviously, the bigger the diamond, the higher its price tag. Cut has to do with how the diamond is faceted to show off its fire and brilliance. The cut of a diamond can either enhance its natural beauty or, if poorly done, smother it.

Taking a rough, or uncut, diamond and transforming it into a gemstone is a painstaking process. A rough diamond can be hard to distinguish from other stones. Only after the process of cleaving, cutting, and polishing is a diamond transformed into a dazzling gem. Before a diamond cutter can begin, he or she will carefully examine the stone to see how it can best be cut to maximize its beauty and value. It is easier and less wasteful to split the diamond along planes that are naturally weaker, so diamond cutters first divide the stone along those lines. Then, following a carefully devised plan, the cutter will make facets. Often, about half the diamond is cut away during this process. The most popular design, the "brilliant" cut, usually has 58 facets and allows the stone to reflect the maximum amount of light.

While the diamonds most people are familiar with are in the form of gems, not all diamonds are processed into jewelry. In fact, 80 percent of diamonds are used in industrial processes. Diamonds with flaws in color or shape, or without the brilliance and fire necessary to capture the eye and sell as gemstones, are employed in a variety of manufacturing sectors. Some are used as a single crystal, while others are ground into a fine powder and applied to saw blades and the tips of drills. Because diamonds are so hard, they can cut, scratch, scrape, and drill through all other surfaces. Diamonds are used not only in mining, but also in the oil and gas industries, electronics, and even dentistry.

In an effort to keep up with the demand for diamonds, synthetic diamonds have been developed. The majority of these synthetic diamonds are suitable only for industrial purposes. Only 10 percent of industrial-grade diamonds are natural diamonds; the other 90 percent are synthetic. Some artificial diamonds are also used for jewelry.
Diamonds are known all over the world as precious stones that symbolize love and romance. But diamonds also have strength beneath their beauty. The diamond is much more than just another pretty face.

An old saying goes: "One man’s meat is another man’s poison." In much the same way, nuclear technology brings to mind different things for different people. To some, it is a useful tool in medicine and an efficient source of energy. To others, it conjures up images of mushroom clouds and mass destruction.

Understanding nuclear technology begins with the nucleus, the heart of the atom. All matter is made up of atoms, and every atom consists of particles called neutrons, protons, and electrons. Neutrons and protons form the solid nucleus of the atom, while the much smaller electrons orbit the nucleus like the planets around the sun. The number of these three particles in an atom determines what kind of matter, or element, it is. For instance, carbon has six protons, six neutrons, and six electrons.

The ratio of these particles within an atom determines whether the atom is stable. Nature does not like instability, so unstable atoms undergo a natural process called "radioactive decay," in which they release extra particles. Radioactive decay can change an atom from one element into another element or into another form of the same element, which is known as an isotope. Isotopes occur when the number of neutrons present in the nucleus differs. Carbon-14, for example, is an isotope of carbon with eight neutrons instead of six.

The particles released by radioactive decay can be harmful, but they can be put to good use as well. In the field of nuclear medicine, radiation is used to treat cancer. Radioactive elements can also be injected into the body and tracked with imaging equipment to provide a look inside the body without surgery. This procedure is very useful in medical diagnosis. When the United States’ Food and Drug Administration tests new drugs for safety, many of the tests are conducted using nuclear processes. Carbon dating is another technique that relies on nuclear processes. In the field of archaeology, it is used to determine the age of artifacts based on the radioactive decay of carbon-14. Because the carbon-14 isotope decays into carbon-12 at a very slow and constant rate, you can determine the age of an object by measuring the amount of carbon-14 it contains. Museums also use carbon dating to verify the age of pieces of art. Nuclear technology is present even in our everyday lives. Many smoke detectors, for example, employ a radioactive material to trigger the alarm.

In addition to releasing particles, radioactive decay also releases energy. Uranium, a much heavier radioactive element than carbon-14, is the one most often used to produce nuclear power. One of its isotopes, uranium-235 (U-235), can be induced to split in a process called nuclear fission. If a free neutron hits a U-235 nucleus, the atom will absorb the neutron but will become unstable. It will then split in order to stabilize itself. Each split releases several neutrons, which cause more fission reactions, in turn releasing more neutrons—igniting a chain reaction. This process releases great amounts of energy.

Nuclear power plants use this energy to produce electricity. The energy of the chain reaction is used to create steam to turn a turbine, just as in other power stations. One pound of uranium, however, is able to produce 3.7 million times as much energy as a pound of coal. Plutonium, an element that is formed in uranium-based nuclear reactions, can also be used for fission, making nuclear energy very efficient.

Nuclear power accounts for 17 percent of the world’s electricity, and many people see it as a viable alternative to fossil fuels. Our earth has only a limited amount of coal and oil left, but uranium is abundant. In addition, a well-designed and maintained nuclear power plant produces clean electricity. In fact, a coal-fired plant may disperse more radioactive substances into the atmosphere than a properly functioning nuclear facility. Plants that burn fossil fuels also eject tons of other pollutants, such as carbon dioxide, sulfur, and ash, into the atmosphere each year. Nuclear stations do not release these pollutants.

There are, however, disadvantages to nuclear power. Exposure to radioactive particles can cause radiation sickness and lead to cancer or other health problems. Many precautions are taken to ensure that nuclear reactors are safe. Since particles released by radioactive decay cannot penetrate thick concrete, reactors are encased in concrete buildings that act as shields. However, despite the numerous safety measures taken at nuclear power plants, history has shown that accidents happen. In 1979, radiation leaked from the Three-Mile Island Nuclear Generating Station in the U.S., and thousands of people had to be evacuated. Luckily, no one died. In 1986, an accidental explosion at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Station in the former Soviet Union was not contained, and thousands of civilians and military personnel were exposed to radiation. Thirty people died from the explosion or soon after, and within the next several years, thousands more experienced a variety of health problems due to the radiation they received.

In recent years, many people have also become concerned that nuclear reactors are vulnerable to attack. A bomb or sabotage at a nuclear facility could cause a horrendous disaster, as the accident at Chernobyl has shown. Not surprisingly, the risks associated with nuclear power have given rise to the expression "NIMBY," an acronym for "not in my backyard." This phrase captures the sentiments of much of the public. Although people appreciate the electricity a nuclear reactor provides, they do not want a potential radioactive "bomb" near their homes.

The NIMBY sentiment applies even more to the disposal of nuclear waste. Waste products from nuclear reactors are highly radioactive and cannot be simply thrown away. Even though containers for nuclear waste are designed to stop radioactive leaks, the material inside can remain toxic for thousands of years. Even the strongest containers will deteriorate and fail before the material is safe. Used fuel rods from nuclear reactors are cooled in tightly sealed containers in pools of water for several years and then buried deep underground. There is no guarantee, however, that measures like these will be enough to protect people and the environment.

Nuclear technology poses another less direct, but equally important risk—nuclear proliferation. Although nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants require different grades of uranium, the technology used to produce nuclear power can also be used to develop weapons capable of killing millions of people. The two superpowers of the cold war, the U.S. and Russia, have enough nuclear bombs to kill every person on earth many times over. As more nations acquire nuclear power and possibly nuclear weapons, the likelihood of a devastating nuclear war increases.

Clearly, nuclear technology has advantages and disadvantages, and there is a heated debate about its use. As the countries of the world plan for a cleaner, safer, and more energy-efficient future, they must weigh the pros and cons of this technology carefully.

Since the dawn of human history, people have looked up at the stars and longed to reach them. With the recent advances in mathematics and physics, scientists have been able to invent and build vehicles to take humans far above Earth and into space. Science-fiction writers often imagine these people living in space stations—enormous, rotating habitats teeming with activity. In reality, a program began in the 1980s to build a simpler, more basic facility that has become known as the International Space Station.

A space station is a structure orbiting Earth that human beings can inhabit for extended periods of time. Since 1971, nine space stations have been launched into orbit and occupied by astronauts. Some of these stations have been built by the Soviet Union and others by the United States. The International Space Station is unique in that it is the result of cooperation between many countries.

During the height of the cold war in 1961, U.S. President John F. Kennedy vowed to put a man on the moon before the decade was over. The U.S. succeeded in sending astronauts to the moon on July 20, 1969. But the financial burden of putting astronauts on the moon meant that the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) had to postpone some of its plans. It wasn’t until after the cold war had ended, in 1991, that plans for the International Space Station began to materialize.

In 1993, U.S. President Bill Clinton urged NASA to join forces with its Russian counterpart. One of the trickiest parts of combining the efforts of these two former rivals was learning how to work together after having had separate space programs and not having shared knowledge for the previous thirty years. The Russians had succeeded in sending up and occupying several space stations for varying lengths of time. The U.S., on the other hand, had concentrated on developing the space shuttle, an airplane-like vehicle that could be used multiple times to carry passengers into space and back. The integration of the two nations’ space programs began when NASA’s space shuttles began to ferry American astronauts to the already orbiting Russian space station, Mir, in 1995. This allowed American astronauts to learn the practical know-how of operating and occupying a space station. Russian astronauts, on the other hand, benefited because they were finally able to complete the structure of Mir with the funding they received from the U.S.

In November 1998, the first module of the International Space Station was launched on top of a Russian rocket. Due to growing international cooperation, this component, called Zarya, which means "sunrise" in Russian, had been built in Russia using American funding and technology.

A little bigger than a standard bus, Zarya was designed to provide electricity and propulsion for the International Space Station, but it did not include living quarters for crew members. Next, the American space shuttle Endeavour met up with Zarya and attached the U.S. connection module Unity. Finally, another Russian module was attached to the ISS. Called Zvezda, meaning "star," this structure was the crew living area.

In October 2000, Expedition One, the first ISS crew, consisting of two Russians and one American, arrived. Expedition Two included a woman astronaut, and subsequent expeditions have included crew members from countries such as Spain and Brazil. The International Space Station is the product of the cooperation of nearly twenty space agencies around the world.

In 2001, the space shuttle Atlantis delivered a laboratory called Destiny to the International Space Station to study the effects of zero gravity. Destiny was a monumental step for the ISS because it had the facilities to conduct scientific experiments that could lead to a deeper understanding of the effects of long-term space travel. Much of the research being done in the ISS has to do with zero gravity and its effects on the human body. Zero gravity, or the weightlessness that humans experience in outer space, feels like constantly falling from a great height or riding a roller coaster.

Scientists have discovered that in a weightless environment, bodily fluids tend to stay in the upper body. Many astronauts have shown a decrease in strength in their lower body as well as a significant loss of bone calcium after long periods of weightlessness.

The number of red blood cells in the bloodstream, those that deliver oxygen to the body’s tissues, also goes down, which can lead to a variety of health problems. When astronauts began to do certain exercises on specially designed machines while living in the ISS, the negative effects of zero gravity on their bodies were reduced.

As scientists study how weightlessness affects the human body, they are also conducting many other experiments. By studying how proteins, viruses, and living cells behave in space, scientists may be able to develop more effective medicines. Observing how fluids and flames behave differently when they’re not subject to Earth’s gravity can lead to new alloys and other materials for industrial use. Last but not least, watching Earth from space allows scientists to document the effects of environmental damage, volcanic eruptions, pollution, and many other factors.

Since the addition of Destiny, several European countries, as well as the Japanese space agency, have contributed other components to the ISS. It now has docking compartments, robotic arms, solar panels, and an array of other gadgets that allow astronauts to perform safer space walks, and of course, conduct more scientific experiments. The International Space Station also has a "lifeboat" in the form of a Russian Soyuz spacecraft that could return the crew to Earth in the case of an emergency.

Since 1998, most of the U.S. space shuttles’ flights have been used to work on the ISS. The progress of the space station has come at a price, however. Sadly, in 2003, the space shuttle Columbia disintegrated as it was returning from orbit, and all seven crew members aboard died. The shuttle fleet was grounded, which left the International Space Station’s development virtually at a standstill until 2005. Since then, construction has picked up but proceeds more slowly than before the Columbia disaster. There were only four space shuttle flights to the ISS between 2005 and June 2007. Even at this reduced pace, however, the ISS is expected to be mostly completed by 2010.

Although the development of the ISS has slowed down, there has been some growth in the area of space tourism. A man named Denis Tito made world history on April 28, 2001, when he became the first paying passenger to travel to the International Space Station for the price of twenty million dollars.

Some argue that while there are still so many problems on Earth, we should not be using valuable resources for space exploration. While they may have a valid point that the budget set aside for space exploration and research could be used to fight crime, reduce poverty, and improve social welfare systems, space exploration has improved the quality of our lives. Many of the technologies originally developed for the space program have practical applications on Earth, such as water-purification treatments and scratch-resistant lenses for eyeglasses.

Perhaps in the future, humans will be able to travel to the far corners of the galaxy. Today, however, they can hope for a better future in seeing that because of international cooperation, a project that was not feasible for a single nation to manage has been accomplished by many working together.

Although fewer than two hundred years have passed since the first man set foot on Antarctica, this frozen southern continent has been the center of a great deal of controversy. Countries have fought over the right to claim it as their own, military forces have hoped to use it as a stronghold, and modern businesses want to exploit its natural resources for profit. With so many competing interests at stake, Antarctica is carefully managed by a team of international legal experts. As a result, even though fewer than a thousand people actually make Antarctica their home, its frigid shores and vast glaciers have earned it a prominent position in the minds of people all over the world.

An American seal hunter named John Davis was probably the first man to land on Antarctica, in 1821. Rumors of a southern landmass, however, had been circulating since antiquity.
