It can squeeze itself into almost any opening and wait for prey to approach. A crab might be crawling near the reef, only to be captured by the octopus’ eight tentacles and quickly eaten.

After taking many photographs, John surfaced. Every photograph of a coral reef is valuable, for there may come a time when coral reefs are extinct. Coral polyps and coral algae are sensitive to temperature, and global warming is heating the ocean, making it harder for reefs to grow. Some divers chip off pieces of the reefs to take home. Some people poison the water near the reefs in order to collect the beautiful fish and sell them for aquariums. The poison only paralyzes the fish, but it kills the corals. Even worse, some fishermen use dynamite near coral reefs. The fish are killed and float to the surface, while huge parts of the coral reef are damaged. Many coral reefs are shrinking; they are being damaged faster than they can grow.

John hopes that more people learn to appreciate the beauty and importance of coral reefs. Perhaps then, he thinks, more people will work to save the reefs, and future generations will always be able to visit the marvelous underwater world of the ocean’s coral reefs.

Rebecca Clark could hardly wait to exit the small airplane. She got out, darted through the snow, and hugged her father. Rebecca was very excited to see him again. This was her first visit to the Arctic, where Dr. Clark had been working as a polar scientist for over three months.

Rebecca knew from her father’s research that the Arctic is the most northern part of the planet. Not many people live there because the weather is very cold most of the year. The Arctic has the longest winters and the shortest summers. It also has the longest days and the longest nights. In the summer, the sun shines almost all the time, and in the winter, the night can last up to six months.

Rebecca's father and his team had brought lots of fresh food with them. This was because the Arctic soil, called permafrost, is permanently frozen, making it impossible for trees, vegetables, or fruit to grow. The scientists had enough supplies to last them, but there was nothing Rebecca's father wanted more than a visit from his daughter. He was eager to tell her about his Arctic adventures. They settled in his cabin and warmed up with some tea.
"Dad, did you make it to the North Pole?" asked Rebecca.
"Yes, but I didn't walk there; I flew over it in a special airplane," he said.
Rebecca was curious. "Can you walk to the North Pole?"

"Yes," he replied, "but it is very hard to do, and many have died trying. As you know, Rebecca, the North Pole is a very difficult place to visit. For centuries the North Pole remained one of the last unconquered places on Earth. People tried to see what was at the top of our planet, but they were unable to cross the many kilometers of ice and snow. In the 1500s, explorers from Holland and England were trying to find a new route to Asia, and they thought that going through the Arctic Ocean would shorten the way. A few explorers tried this route, but their ships got stuck in the ice. They returned home discouraged, and some explorers looked for other routes to the riches of Asia. Most explorers forgot about the Arctic. It wasn't until the late 1800s that the golden age of Arctic exploration began."
"Why did people try again?" asked Rebecca.

"Well, even though explorers were no longer looking for a passage to Asia, they were seeking personal glory," explained Dr. Clark. "Navigating a route through the Arctic and conquering the North Pole would give any explorer fame and fortune and would bring prestige to his country. So the race was on."
"What do you mean?" asked Rebecca.

"In 1893 the Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen was the first to break through the ice and get very close to the North Pole. His famous ship, called the Fram , was especially designed for traveling through thick sea ice. Nansen got as far as he could, and when the Fram couldn't push through the ice anymore, he set out to reach the North Pole on foot. He took one of his crewmen with him, and they proceeded on sleds pulled by dogs. Exhausted after many days, they could go no further. They left the Norwegian flag at 86°14' N, which was the most northern latitude any explorer had ever reached. Fridtjof Nansen became a hero, but the North Pole had not been conquered yet."
"So who made it first?" Rebecca asked as she poured more tea.
"This is debatable," her father answered. "Two explorers claimed to reach the pole first.

Robert Peary, a brave American who was obsessed with exploring the North Pole, led numerous expeditions across the Arctic. He finally succeeded in his quest in 1909. Peary learned to adapt to life in the frozen north from the Inuit people. They are often called Eskimos and have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years. They taught Peary how to dress warmly with sealskin and accompanied him on his expeditions. Finally, on his last expedition, together with his most trusted crew member, Matthew Henson, and fifty Inuit helpers, Peary crossed the Arctic and reached the North Pole.

Upon his return to the United States, however, Peary learned some terrible news. Frederick Cook, another American explorer, was claiming that he had already reached the North Pole—one year before Peary. No one could prove which of the two explorers, if either of them, had actually reached the pole. It was tricky because back then there was no way of communicating with explorers so far north, and their expeditions could last a year or longer. Also, explorers had very primitive ways of figuring out their position. They used an instrument called a sextant to measure how far the sun rose above the horizon, which in turn told how far north or south they were. A sextant combines a telescope, a ruler, and a mirror, and requires skill to use accurately."
"Then what happened?" asked Rebecca.

"Both men insisted they were right, and a scandal erupted," replied Dr. Clark. "In the end, the National Geographic Society backed Peary's claim of reaching the North Pole. But even today, some still question whether Peary really succeeded."
"Why do people doubt him?" asked Rebecca.
"Robert Peary was a great explorer," explained her father, "but not a very good navigator. Some people thought he had read his instruments wrong when he claimed that he was at the North Pole."
"How about you, Dad? What do you use when you go exploring?" Rebecca asked.

"Today life in the Arctic is very different from what it was one hundred years ago," said her father. "We use airplanes, submarines, and special ships called icebreakers to visit the North Pole. Since Peary's trip, there have been hundreds of Arctic expeditions. We use computers and satellite telephones to keep in touch. Many scientists spend months in the Arctic doing tests, collecting data, and researching different scientific occurrences."

"Just like you, right, Dad?" Rebecca said. She looked out the window at the pale sun, still shining in the late Arctic evening. "And me," she added with a wide smile. "I’m going to be a polar scientist when I grow up too!"

In 1609 Galileo turned his telescope to the heavens. He looked at Jupiter and was astonished; he saw four moons orbiting the planet. As the centuries passed, people invented larger and more powerful telescopes. But these improvements could not satisfy their curiosity about the other planets that orbit our sun. Instead of improving telescopes on Earth, scientists thought, why not send telescopes to the planets?

In 1977 the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) sent two probes, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, to explore the mysterious planets beyond Mars. These four planets are called gas giants, and they are about 60 to 1,300 times the size of Earth. Both Voyager 1 and 2 explored the closest two, Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 also studied Saturn’s moon Titan, while Voyager 2 traveled on to study the planets Uranus and Neptune.

From January to April of 1979, Voyager 1 photographed and studied Jupiter and its many moons (scientists keep discovering new ones). Beautiful pictures were sent to Earth, allowing scientists to research the complicated weather systems that wrap around the planet. Jupiter's atmosphere to core temperatures can range from -145 to +24,000 degrees Celsius. Jupiter has lightning and its own auroral phenomenon, just like Earth’s northern lights.

When images of one of Jupiter’s moons, Io, were sent back to Earth, scientists were astonished. Moons, it was believed, could not have volcanoes because they were too small and cold. But Io has volcanoes more violent than any on Earth, with eruptions that send material three hundred kilometers high. Later, scientists realized that because Jupiter is so big, its gravity pulls the side of the moon closest to Jupiter more strongly than the opposite side. As Io rotates, its different parts are constantly stretched and pulled, and this creates heat. For example, if you take a metal spoon and bend it back and forth, the place where it bends becomes hot.

Jupiter’s gravity is so powerful that it bends the interior of its moons. Scientists call this process tidal heating. On Jupiter’s moon Io, tidal heating is powerful enough to cause eruptions hundreds of times larger than any volcano on Earth. The Voyager probes also discovered that Jupiter’s moon Europa has a surface of ice. If tidal heating warms Europa’s interior enough to melt the ice, is it possible that life exists in vast oceans underneath its icy surface? Scientists are now designing probes to land on Europa to answer this question.

From Earth, Saturn and its rings appear peaceful and beautiful, but the Voyager probes discovered something different. Saturn has violent windstorms over 1,400 kilometers per hour, and its rings are not the perfectly smooth objects we see through telescopes. Some rings have gaps, like a necklace missing a few pearls. But strangest of all, the rings have patterns in them that look like braided hair. Scientists believe that the uneven orbits of Saturn’s small moons cause these strange patterns, and the gaps as well.

Voyager 1 also studied Titan, a large moon that orbits Saturn. Titan is the only moon in the solar system to have an atmosphere. Voyager 1 found that Titan’s atmosphere is made mostly of nitrogen, while the surface is a mixture of ice and rock. Before there was life on Earth, its atmosphere was also mostly nitrogen. Some scientists believe that when we look at Titan, we are seeing what Earth looked like far in the past.

In 1986 Voyager 2 arrived at Uranus and discovered a shocking mystery that is unexplained to this day. Most planets, like Earth, spin on their axes vertically. Their north and south poles point up and down compared to the rest of the solar system. Uranus is the opposite. Its axis lines up horizontally, so that one pole faces toward the sun and the other away from the sun. This strange fact had long been known, but Voyager 2 discovered a stranger contradiction. Even though the equator of Uranus receives almost no sunlight, its equator is always as hot as, or hotter than, the polar region that directly faces the sun.

Voyager 2 arrived at Neptune in 1989. It discovered six moons orbiting Neptune, as well as a faint ring system around the planet. Neptune is a beautiful world, a deep blue color with giant white clouds of methane rising and falling, just as water does in Earth’s atmosphere. After its mission to Neptune, Voyager 2 began to travel out of the solar system.

The success of the Voyager missions encouraged scientists to send more probes to explore our solar system. The Cassini-Huygens spaceship, after traveling for seven years, is now orbiting and studying Saturn. In 2004 NASA landed two rovers on Mars. These small, six-wheeled, solar-powered vehicles are sending back pictures and doing tests on Martian rocks. Since the Voyager probes were launched in 1977, NASA, the European Space Agency, and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency have sent more than 35 new missions to explore the inner and outer planets, the moon, asteroids, comets, and the sun.

Today both Voyager 1 and 2 are on their way out of the solar system. Voyager 1 is over 16 billion kilometers from Earth and is the most distant man-made object in the universe. But the missions of these pioneering probes continue. They are now studying the complex area of space where our solar system ends and the rest of the universe begins.

In addition to their scientific missions, Voyager 1 and 2 may play a much more important role in humanity’s exploration of space. Both probes carry a gold-plated disc containing messages from Earth. If aliens ever find a Voyager probe, they will be able to hear the natural sounds of our planet, a selection of music, and greetings in over fifty languages. But perhaps the most important message is not on the discs at all. Both spaceships are themselves a statement about one of humanity’s best qualities: curiosity. Like Galileo, many of us on Earth want to see farther and understand what we see.
Mark’s father parked his car. "There’s a crowd forming around Old Faithful," he said. "The geyser is probably about to blow. Come on, Mark! If we hurry, we might get to see the eruption."

Mark had never seen a geyser erupt, so he and his father had come to Yellowstone National Park for the day. The park was famous for its geysers and hot springs, especially the geyser known as Old Faithful.

Mark’s dad had told him that geysers are one of the most amazing things found in nature. A crack in the ground is filled with hot water, with bubbles and steam rising to the surface. Then—often with little warning—it erupts. A giant burst of steam and water shoots high into the air.
Mark and his father made it to the geyser just in time.
"Old Faithful is about to blow!" a park ranger shouted.
Mark felt a vibration coming from deep beneath the earth. There was a strange gurgling sound, and then, from a hole in the ground, steam and water shot up over forty meters into the air!
"Whoa!" Mark cried.
Soon the water flowed back down into the hole. To Mark, it sounded just like water gurgling down the drain of a sink.

Mark had a question for the ranger. "Why is this geyser named Old Faithful?" he asked. "Most geysers are unpredictable," the ranger explained. "But Old Faithful’s eruptions follow a predictable pattern. If it erupts for two minutes, then it erupts again in sixty minutes. If it erupts for five minutes, it erupts again in one hundred minutes."
"I get it," said Mark. "Old Faithful always does the same thing!"
"Exactly." The ranger grinned at Mark.
Soon Mark and his father followed the park ranger to an exhibit. There, Mark learned that Yellowstone Park contains more than half of all the geysers and hot springs on earth.
"What are hot springs?" Mark asked the ranger. "Are they different from geysers?"

"Yes, they are different," the ranger replied. "They form because of earth's water table. When rain falls, some water sinks deep into the earth until it reaches a layer of rock. The water sits on top of the rock and forms what’s called the water table—a layer of water.

"In some places, such as Yellowstone Park, the hot core of the earth is near this water table. So the water gets heated to boiling hot temperatures. If there is a crack in the earth above the water, the water expands and forces its way up. Water then pools around the opening."
"I see." Mark nodded. "Hot springs don’t erupt. But then what makes geysers erupt?"

"Well," the park ranger said. "A hot spring’s crack, or fissure, is shaped like a pipe. But a geyser’s fissure is wider, forming a large cavern underground. Hot water and steam rise and fill the cavern while the water at the top of the cavern cools off quickly. This cool water acts like a heavy lid on a pot of boiling water. Hot pressure builds up in the cavern. Suddenly all the pressure is released at once, shooting water and steam into the air."

Mark and his father stayed a while longer, exploring the exhibit. They found out that Iceland, a small country in Europe, also has a large number of geysers and hot springs. The people living there can even use the energy from geysers and hot springs to heat their homes and generate electricity!
"Look, Dad!" Mark pointed to a picture of a giant mud bath. "Sometimes the hot spring mixes with soil to form mud baths like this one. I bet it feels good to lay in that!"

"Many people find these mud baths soothing," replied Mark's dad. "Japan is famous for its relaxing hot springs. Some people even believe that mud baths and hot springs can cure diseases—or at least take away some aches and pains!"
The ranger heard them talking. "In Yellowstone Park the hot springs’ water is usually too hot to touch," he said. "So unfortunately, people can’t bathe in the hot springs here.

"But there is something special about our hot springs. Some forms of bacteria and algae live in them. These life forms are different colors and give the hot springs an unusual and beautiful appearance."
Later Mark and his father thanked the park ranger and headed back toward their car. It was time to go home.
"Dad, I wish we could go to one of those hot springs where you can swim and relax," Mark said. "That sounds like fun!"
"I’ve heard there are hot springs like that in Canada," replied Mark’s father. "You can sit in a hot spring high in the mountains. Would you like to go there on our next vacation?" he asked.
"Yes!" Mark said, grinning. "That sounds cool . . . er, I mean, hot!"

Notice that summer seems longer nowadays? The average temperature has increased over the past one hundred years, but changes in the earth’s climate are not new. The earth's climate has changed constantly over its five-billion-year history. Sometimes, the climate has warmed up so much that the oceans have risen and covered the earth. These changes are extreme, but they usually occurred gradually over many thousands of years. The first modern humans inhabited the earth between fifteen thousand and thirty thousand years ago, when most land was covered in ice. Fourteen thousand years ago, the last ice sheet began to melt; seven thousand years ago, the ice was gone. When the "Ice Age" ended, the earth was a different place. Many kinds of plants and animals had become extinct. However, the Ice Age was not the last example of extreme climate change.

The Europeans lived through a "Little Ice Age" that began in the fourteenth century and lasted for five hundred years. During the Little Ice Age, winters were bitterly cold in many parts of the world, but climate changes were most thoroughly documented in Europe and North America. In the mid-seventeenth century, glaciers in the Swiss Alps grew in size, gradually crushing entire villages. The River Thames in London and the canals of the Netherlands often froze over during the winter. Sea ice surrounding Iceland extended for miles in every direction, and ships could no longer dock at its harbors. There were many years of death and famine due to short crop seasons. In 1850, the world's climate began warming again and the Little Ice Age came to an end.

Over the last century, the earth has undergone severe climate change again—but this time around, it’s not getting colder, it’s getting warmer. The earth has warmed about 1˚Fahrenheit, and the four warmest years of the twentieth century all happened in the 1990s. This phenomenon is commonly known as "climate change." Although the earth’s climate has drastically altered in the past, the recent climate change is different in two ways. First, almost all scientists agree that we humans are to blame in some way, and, second, climate change is occurring at an unprecedented pace. Climate change and its causes, effects, and solutions have become a major issue for all generations. In a recent survey in Britain, young people said that global warming was their biggest concern for the world’s future, even more than the threat of terrorism or lack of housing.

Why is the earth’s climate changing? This issue is hotly debated, but most scientists agree that humans are responsible. The main human activity that negatively affects our climate is the emission of carbon dioxide gas (CO₂) into the earth’s atmosphere. When power plants burn coal, oil, and natural gas to make electricity, they emit CO₂, and when we use a car, bus, or plane, they burn gasoline in their engines and emit CO₂. Too much CO₂in the atmosphere means that the "greenhouse effect" cannot function normally. The greenhouse effect is a natural process in which sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the earth’s surface. In turn, the land and oceans release heat into the atmosphere. Water vapor, CO₂, and some other gases absorb some of this heat, and the atmosphere warms up. The rest of the heat goes into space. If there is too much CO₂ in the atmosphere, too much heat remains in the atmosphere and so the earth’s climate becomes warmer. And a warmer earth has many consequences.

The effects of climate change are all around us—some are subtle and some are very obvious. Something that everyone is feeling is hotter weather, called "global warming," with 1998 being the warmest year on record, and 2002 and 2003 tying for second warmest. In Europe in 2003, 27,000 people died in heat waves. Eleven thousand Tuvaluans live on nine coral atolls, totaling ten square miles, east of Australia. Tuvalu has no industry and burns little petroleum, yet this tiny country is on the front line of climate change. Rising sea levels mean that Tuvalu may be completely submerged and then disappear like the lost city of Atlantis. In 2002, Prime Minister Koloa Talake announced plans to sue the United States and Australia at the International Court of Justice in the Hague over their disproportionate production of carbon dioxide emissions.

In Antarctica and the Arctic, climate change has reduced the thickness of ice by 40 percent. Recent changes mean that polar bears may become extinct in this century if weather trends continue. All kinds of animals and their habits—where they live, what they eat, when they breed—are affected by the warm weather. Another major consequence of global warming is extreme weather. Floods and storms are occurring with increasing intensity. For example, in 2004, Australia had its worst drought in one hundred years and, during severe tropical storms, experienced hailstones the size of tennis balls—the biggest in history. In Canada, data collected from insurance companies showed that over the past thirty years, more natural catastrophes occurred there than ever before. With such noticeable changes in the earth’s climates, governments have started to take action.

World leaders are slowly acknowledging the existence of climate change and the fact that humans are to blame, but so far, they have been slow to act. The most famous international treaty on global warming is the Kyoto Protocol. The 141 nations that signed it in 1998 committed to reducing their country’s emissions of CO₂. Notably, the world’s largest producer of CO₂, the United States, as well as Australia, refused to sign the treaty and have received much criticism internationally. China is the world’s second biggest emitter of CO₂ and has signed the Kyoto Protocol. However, analysts say China faces an uphill battle, with private transport viewed as its major environmental obstacle. The biggest concern is cars—what will happen when every Chinese citizen drives a car? What will happen if citizens of developed countries like France and the United States continue to drive cars all the time?

The good news is that we as individuals can reduce climate change by taking responsibility for our part in global warming, and subsequently changing our patterns of energy use. Here are some suggestions:
1. Tune up your home and make it energy efficient: Heating and cooling our homes, schools, and workplaces use the most energy of all. Use insulation and ventilation.
2. Buy wisely: if you buy a new appliance or machine like a computer, washing machine, freezer, or fridge, choose one that is energy efficient.
3. Leave the car at home—catch public transport, ride a bike, or walk.
4. Grow your own food—the transport, storage, and cooling of food uses an enormous amount of energy.
As American Senator John Kerry remarked, "Climate change is real. The longer we wait, the harder the problem will be to solve."

Every day, people get up, go to school or work, walk, read, and do many other things. Where do we get the energy? The answer lies in what we eat, drink, and breathe; our fuel is food, water, and air. But what about non-living things? What powers a car? What makes water boil? Where does your computer get its energy from?

"I put gasoline in the car, cook over a gas stove, and plug in the computer," you reply. Your answer sums up the main energy sources that power non-living things: oil, gas, and electricity. Oil and gas have two energy uses; the first is to fuel cars, buses, trains, and planes, and the second is to generate electricity. Coal, nuclear power, and hydropower (energy from flowing water) are also used to make electricity.

People in most developed countries use oil for 50% of their energy. Problems arise, however, when we rely so heavily on oil for our energy needs. First of all, there is a limited supply of oil. Oil industry experts estimate that current oil reserves will last for only forty more years. This means that by 2045, there will be no more oil to make gasoline or electricity.

Currently, most of the world's available oil is consumed only by developed countries. Nearly a third of the world's population of 6.1 billion people has no electricity, and another third has only limited access to electricity. Twenty percent of the world's population consumes seventy percent of the world's energy resources. What will happen when developing countries get access to electricity and oil? There simply won't be enough.

Another problem is the location of our energy. As recently as a couple of centuries ago, virtually everyone used fuel that they could find close to home. In the modern world, energy sources are often long distances away from the end user. For example, many countries have no oil reserves and import all of their oil. When oil is transported over long distances, there is the risk of oil spills, which can cause irreversible damage to the natural environment. Conflicts, or even wars, can erupt over the control of oil fields and oil pipelines.

The most serious problem with burning oil for energy is global warming. The earth’s atmosphere is getting hotter because there is too much carbon dioxide (CO2) in the air. Burning fuels like gasoline (to drive cars) and coal (to produce electricity) releases large amounts of CO2 into the air. Scientists predict that global warming may cause sea levels to rise, animals to become extinct, and extreme weather, everything from severe droughts to hurricanes.

The good news is that we don't have to use oil, gas, and coal to produce energy. There are other energy sources that won't run out, don't require transportation across the globe, and don't release CO2. The best thing about energy from these alternative energy sources, also called "renewable energy," is that it is unlimited─it comes from water, wind, and the sun.

Wind power is not new; boats and ships have been using it for thousands of years to travel across the globe. Windmills in Europe have used wind for centuries to pump water, grind grain, and saw wood. In modern times, machines called wind turbines, with blades from one meter to one hundred meters long, turn wind into electricity. Scientists believe that if collections of these turbines were installed in wind farms in the world’s windiest places, there would be enough energy to satisfy global demand.

Solar power is energy from the sun. Energy from the sun can be used in two ways: to make electricity and to heat water. Solar cells are thin pieces of silicon that produce electricity when exposed to sunlight. You may have used a solar-powered calculator or flashlight. Solar cells can also power lights in a home. A solar-powered car has even been built! In Australia, a solar boat was showcased at the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney. The Solar Sailor is powered by solar panels, and its movable, wing-like solar panels also function as sails. The sun's energy can also heat water efficiently and cheaply. Water is passed through solar collectors that concentrate the sun's rays and heat the water; the hot water is then stored in a tank and can be used for bathing or washing dishes.

Other kinds of renewable energy are also under development. One of these comes from biomass, which means organic matter. Wood has been used for thousands of years to create energy, but scientists have discovered that other kinds of organic matter can also be used to create fuel, like certain grasses, trees, plants, or even animal dung. Biomass can be treated and made into fuel, or it can produce electricity as it decomposes.

Another renewable energy source is geothermal energy, energy that comes from inside the earth. For example, steam from geysers and water from hot springs can be used to generate electricity. At geothermal power plants in California, geysers produce steam, which turns electric turbines. Some of these power generators have been operating for over forty years.

Hydrogen is a source of clean energy that is very attractive because it is the most abundant element in the universe. A fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity and heat─and the only by-product is pure water! Hydrogen fuel cells have the potential to replace the engines in vehicles and provide power for cars and buses. Many portable devices could also be powered by these fuel cells, such as laptop computers and cell phones.

A final type of alternative energy source under development is compressed air. Compressed air is the energy source for the "air car," which uses no gasoline. Instead, a tank full of compressed air powers the engine. The tank needs to be refilled at an "air" station. An air car factory has already been established in France, and production will begin soon.

So, if energy from oil, coal, and gas causes problems like pollution and global warming, to name only a few, why don't we switch to renewable energy immediately? Why doesn't every house have solar-heated hot water? Why aren't our computers powered by wind turbines? Why doesn’t everyone drive an air car?

There are a number of reasons. First, renewable energy is currently more expensive than traditional fuels. Second, decades of access to cheap oil have made consumers lazy and apathetic about energy. "There's enough oil now, who cares about the future?" and "As long as my city isn't polluted, it's okay," are common attitudes. Third, at present, the disadvantages of oil are still not grave enough to force citizens or governments to react. Pollution is an ever-increasing problem, but its effects are gradual, and the most severe effects of global warming may not be seen for another fifty years. Finally, companies and governments in the world's most industrialized nations currently earn large profits from the oil, coal, and gas industries. It is not in their interest to switch to renewable energy sources unless the public demands it.

The good news, however, is that many people around the world are changing their habits. For example, some schools, community groups, and small businesses are using wind turbines and solar panels as their sources of electricity. Governments are slowly changing regulations to make it easier for builders to construct homes that rely on renewable energy. The earth has taken good care of us─it gives us clean air, water, and food to eat. By switching to renewable sources of energy, we can start to take care of the earth.

32.title: Apollo 11: A Giant Leap for Mankind

paragraphs.text: People have always looked up at the moon with wonder. Ancient people worshipped the moon as a goddess, and many believed that she was responsible for the creation of time. The first calendars were based on the phases of the moon, which change consistently to complete a full cycle every 28 days. In the moon’s bright features, people have imagined a human face, a rabbit, and even a round piece of cheese. It was not until the twentieth century, however, that the United States and the Soviet Union began to develop technology that would allow humans to visit the alluring white sphere. Both countries were set on conquering outer space; both wanted to prove their scientific superiority and their military strength. This "space race," as it became known, served to fuel people’s interest in the moon.

The first major hurdle to space travel was overcome by the Soviet Union in 1957 with the launch of the first artificial satellite. Sputnik, as it was called, was catapulted into orbit by a rocket. It weighed about 83 kilograms and looked like a giant ball with several antennas that protruded out like whiskers on a cat’s nose. It also had two radio transmitters attached to its spherical body that sent out signals, helping Soviet scientists learn more about the density of space. After completing its task, Sputnik was brought back toward the earth, but was destroyed upon reentry into the atmosphere.

Despite the loss of Sputnik, the experiment was considered a great success. As a result, the Soviets attempted several more satellite launches, including one that took a dog, named Laika, up into space. Laika became the first living creature from Earth to travel into orbit.

The first human to leave Earth’s atmosphere was also part of the Soviet team, Colonel Yuri Gagarin. In 1961, Gagarin was chosen to command a space capsule called Vostok 1 . It blasted off from a secret launch pad located in Soviet Kazakhstan. It traveled a complete circle around the earth in just 108 minutes. Then, it returned to the ground over Russia. Before it landed, Gagarin ejected from the capsule and parachuted to safety. After this adventurous ride, many Soviets started to call Gagarin "the Columbus of the Cosmos."

Meanwhile, the United States was trying desperately to match the success of the Soviet space program. Unfortunately, their first attempt to launch a satellite had ended in an explosion on the launch pad. But this did not deter the Americans, and soon after Gagarin’s historic flight, they launched their own manned mission, Freedom 7 , carrying Alan Shepard into space. Shepard, who had been a navy test pilot, earned the distinction of being the first astronaut to return safely with his ship without having to use a parachute. This inspired a second mission, Friendship 7 , piloted by astronaut John Glenn.

With this limited amount of manned space experience, American President John F. Kennedy announced that his country would embark on a new space program managed by their aeronautics agency, NASA. He made a promise to the American public that, before the end of the decade, the country would send an astronaut to the moon and return him to the earth unharmed. This program was named Apollo after the Greek god of the sun, and work began immediately.

The initial stage was to determine how NASA engineers should build a space shuttle that would reach the moon while keeping costs low and minimizing risk to human life. After much debate, they decided to focus on constructing an Apollo spacecraft that consisted of four main sections. The Command Module was the part where the astronauts would sit when the spacecraft was launched and where they would spend most of their time while on board. The Service Module contained all of their equipment, such as oxygen tanks and the engine. The Lunar Module was a small part of the ship that could detach from the main spacecraft. It was the section that would actually land on the moon. The final section, the Launch Escape Tower, would be used during the launch and would be discarded shortly after takeoff. Altogether, the four sections fit together to look like a long, thin rocket with a wide, round tailpipe.

For several years, engineers worked hard to design a fully functioning Apollo spacecraft. In the beginning, the program suffered some setbacks. During a test of Apollo 1 , an explosion resulted in a fire that killed three astronauts on the launch pad. This was devastating to the program, so engineers decided to focus on testing unmanned flights until they were certain that no more astronauts would be harmed. After six major tests, in 1968, the Americans were ready to allow astronauts to pilot spacecraft again. Human-piloted Apollo 7 circled the moon in October of that year, and three more manned missions were launched to test various sections of the spacecraft. Then, in 1969, NASA announced that it was prepared to reach the moon.

Commander Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Buzz Aldrin were chosen for the mission, Apollo 11 . Like Alan Shepard, Armstrong was a navy test pilot with a lot of experience flying experimental airplanes. He had previously worked on other American space missions and was known to cope well with periods of extreme stress. Armstrong would command the crew, Collins would pilot the Command Module (called Columbia ), and Aldrin would be responsible for piloting the Lunar Module (called the Eagle ).

Apollo 11 was launched from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 1:32 pm on July 16, 1969. After four days of travel, it began orbiting the moon. When the spacecraft was in position, Aldrin and Armstrong climbed into the Eagle and separated from Columbia . "The Eagle has wings," Armstrong reported to ground control.

The descent to the moon took almost three hours and the landing was full of tension. The Eagle was coming in too fast, and the flight controllers back on Earth thought the astronauts would have to abort. Armstrong saw that they were heading for a field of boulders. He took manual control of the craft and began skimming across the surface to find a better spot. Moments later, with only thirty seconds of fuel remaining, the Eagle’s footpads touched the moon’s surface in the Sea of Tranquility. From inside the Eagle , Buzz Aldrin confirmed the successful touchdown with the words, "Tranquility base. The Eagle has landed." After several hours, Armstrong crawled out of the hatch and climbed down the outside ladder. From the bottom rung, he jumped the last three feet down to the moon and declared: "That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

With these words, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the moon. First, Armstrong took photographs and soil samples in case the mission had to be aborted suddenly. Then, he and Aldrin, who had climbed down after him, jumped across the landscape and planted the American flag. They also unveiled a plaque that read, "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon. July 1969 AD. We came in peace for all mankind."

When Apollo 11 returned safely to Earth on July 24, the astronauts were welcomed as heroes. Kennedy’s promise had been fulfilled and NASA had achieved a miraculous feat. Ancient people probably never imagined that a human would ever walk on the moon. But, Apollo 11 turned distant dreams into reality, bringing the ancient moon goddess firmly within grasp.

Welcome to my forest. It is autumn, so it is very wonderful here. All the animals, including squirrels like me, are busy getting ready for winter. Look around you and you will see that the leaves on the trees have changed colors. The maple trees have turned bright red, and the elm trees have turned brown and yellow.

Have you ever wondered why the green leaves change into so many different colors? Well, in the spring and summer when the leaves are fresh, they are filled with something called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the natural coloring in the leaves that makes them green.

In order to make food, trees need energy from the sun. Chlorophyll collects the energy from the sun and stores it in the leaves. The leaves use this energy to make a liquid sugar, called sap, that the trees use for food.

The trees spend the spring and summer producing food so that they can grow bigger. During the summer months, the trees get taller and wider and they grow more branches and roots. But most importantly, the trees use their energy to grow nuts and fruits for animals like me to eat.

At the end of the summer, things begin to change. It becomes cooler, and there is much less sunlight during the day. Chlorophyll needs the sunlight and cannot survive in the cold weather. So in the autumn when the weather becomes cool, the trees can no longer make chlorophyll. When this happens, the leaves lose their green color.

When the green chlorophyll disappears, the leaves’ other colors can be seen. Trees like elm, birch, and poplar show their yellow and light orange colors. These colors were in the leaves all summer, but because of the green chlorophyll, we could not see them.

Some trees, however, get new bright colors in the fall. For example, maple trees turn bright red, and sumac trees turn dark red. These trees get their color from red pigments that build up in the leaves when the sap stops flowing in the fall. These pigments turn leaves red, pink, and even purple. This natural coloring occurs in trees and other plants. It gives some vegetables, like beets and radishes, their red color. It is also what makes some flower blossoms red and pink.
The red pigments come into the leaves during cool, dry, sunny days. I love to go running through the trees, looking at all the colors. Even on the same tree, not all the leaves have the same color.

On some trees, the top leaves are bright red, but the bottom leaves are almost yellow. This is because the top ones get more sun. On trees near a river, the leaves are not bright because trees that get lots of water do not usually have colorful leaves in the fall. But way up there on the top of a mountain, the leaves get lots of sun and little water, so they are very colorful. Even from year to year, the colors of the leaves change. When autumn is dry and cool, the leaves will have brilliant, shining colors. But when the autumn is cloudy and wet, the leaves will not be as beautiful.

The autumn leaves are beautiful to look at, but they don’t last very long. Without chlorophyll, the leaves cannot live. Soon the leaves must fall off the branches onto the ground. But this is good for squirrels because we love to play and jump in them.

When all the leaves have fallen from the trees, the animals know that winter is coming. We hurry up and pack away all our food, and then we tuck ourselves in our little houses and go to sleep for the winter. The trees also sleep during the winter.

Eventually the leaves that fall from the trees decay and turn into soil that is used during the following years as fertilizer for the trees. You see, one of the beautiful things about nature is that everything works in a cycle. The trees wake up in the spring with fresh new leaves. These leaves grow in the summer, fall in the autumn, and then are turned back into soil so that more leaves can grow the next spring. With the help of chlorophyll, the trees get bigger and stronger every year.
